extracted.intended_audience: scientists and researchers who perform peer review for journals (early-career and experienced peer reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Example open peer reviews of research articles across life/physical/social sciences that illustrate what makes a good review: evaluating relevance, methods, statistics, clarity, interpretation, figures, and providing constructive suggestions. The page is a collection of exemplar review text to teach reviewers how to critique manuscripts effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance / Importance of the question
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper address an interesting and timely question and will it influence thinking in the field? (Example language: 'addresses an interesting and timely question', 'will almost certainly influence our thinking about ...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight why the question matters, link the study to broader literature or practical implications, and explicitly state potential impact. Positive reviews emphasize broad applicability (e.g., paradigms applicable to many rare disease genes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the work novel or proposing a novel solution/approach? (Example language: 'finds a novel solution based on a carefully selected set of rules', 'presents a paradigm that can be broadly and usefully applied')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether methods, hypotheses, or conceptual framing advance the field. Note if novelty relies on fortuitous findings versus generalizable approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title and abstract accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The title and abstract are appropriate for the content of the text. (Example language: 'The title and abstract are appropriate for the content of the text.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm they accurately summarize aims, main methods, key result(s), and conclusions. Recommend edits if they overstate findings or omit key limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall organization and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the article well constructed, logically organized, and readable? (Example language: 'the article is well constructed', 'not always easy readability of the text which establishes unclear logical links between concepts')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out unclear logical links or sections that impede comprehension. Suggest reorganization or clearer transitions, and flag long/unclear passages for revision (minor vs major).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and readability of prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the text readable and are logical links between concepts clear? (Example language: 'not always easy readability of the text', 'establishes unclear logical links between concepts')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend specific edits to improve clarity; identify paragraphs or sentences needing simplification or clearer argumentation. Distinguish readability issues from substantive methodological problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Are experiments designed properly to address the hypothesis? (Examples: questions about unstable baseline recordings, need for more randomization, whether automated device allows necessary protocols, and whether experimental design prevents trivial artefacts)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess controls, randomization, blocking, protocol suitability for intended inferences, and whether the chosen apparatus/protocols permit the analyses claimed. Recommend additional controls or redesigned protocols when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods completeness and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Are methods described clearly and in sufficient detail for replication? (Examples: unclear exactly what data were used, whether distances were measured consistently, whether litter cover recorded as continuous or categorical)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors to clarify sampling procedures, measurement units, specific instruments/settings, data selection/processing steps, and to reference or provide standard protocols where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and correctness of statistical analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the statistical methods correct, assumptions met, and tests appropriate? (Example critiques: incorrect binomial test due to unbalanced design; misuse of ANCOVA when slopes differ; inappropriate retention of non-significant interaction terms; misunderstanding of priors in Bayesian example)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request re-analysis when necessary (e.g., use mixed models for random factors, Johnson–Neyman method for ANCOVA with interactions, correct binomial assumptions). Ask for explicit reporting of tests, assumptions checks, and justification for chosen models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of samples and train/test separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Are data samples independent and is train/test separation appropriate for classification analyses? (Example language: 'random sampling one half of data samples from an EEG trace are not independent data', 'non-independent data for training and testing')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag circular analysis and temporal correlations in time-series data; require appropriate cross-validation or independent data splits (e.g., by recording/session/subject rather than random timepoints) and sanity checks (e.g., label permutations, withheld recordings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness and generalizability of classifiers/algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Do classifiers rely on justified features and are results robust beyond the chosen parameters? (Examples: classifiers seem more accurate than prior parameters but remain indicative; risk that classifiers exploit trivial temporal structure)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for sensitivity analyses, alternative feature sets, validation on independent datasets, explanation of feature selection/curation, and acknowledgement of classifier limitations (statistical versus biological significance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability, noise, and data stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Are recordings/data stable and variable results justified? (Examples: unstable pre-drug recordings, veratridine augmentation ranging widely, resting membrane potential somewhat variable)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request examination of sources of variability (instrumentation, biological variability, perfusion), repeatability measures, and documentation of recording stability durations; suggest method tests (e.g., K+ effects on control channels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate mechanistic inference given methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Are mechanistic claims justified by the experimental protocols and analyses? (Example: for precise mechanistic study, more complicated pulse protocols are mandatory; simple protocols may only support screening claims)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between evidence for screening utility versus mechanistic understanding. Recommend additional experiments or more sophisticated protocols when making mechanistic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls and sanity checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the study include essential controls and sanity checks to exclude artefacts? (Examples: recordings without Sender; reversed labels are insufficient as a control; suggest recordings with no Sender to test trivial decoding)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demand appropriate negative and positive controls, label-shuffling controls adapted to data dependence, and other checks that rule out trivial explanations for positive results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomization and predictability of protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the stimulus/protocol randomization adequate to prevent predictability or confounds? (Example: many recordings had identical initial silence lengths causing alignment and predictability issues)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend randomizing protocol timings and balancing conditions to reduce temporal correlations and predictability; document randomization procedures in Methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant/sample selection and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Are participants/samples appropriate and independent (e.g., not only authors as participants)? (Example: including only authors as participants is highly questionable for experiments of this kind)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request justification of participant selection, disclose when participants are authors, and suggest using naïve participants or independent samples when required by experimental aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and data/code availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Are raw data and analysis code available to enable reproduction and reanalysis? (Example: making raw data public enabled independent reanalysis that revealed analytical flaws)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage deposition of raw data, scripts, and detailed workflows; positive recognition when authors share data. If unavailable, request necessary materials for evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of statistics and post-hoc tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Are statistical results fully reported (e.g., post-hoc comparisons, r-squared, test statistics) and interpreted correctly? (Examples: means/sd reported but no post-hoc test; r-squared interpretation inconsistent with statement)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require full reporting of analyses (test used, degrees of freedom, p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes), and include post-hoc tests where applicable; place linear equations or model parameters in figure captions for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate model structure (fixed vs random effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are factors correctly treated as fixed or random and are appropriate mixed models used? (Example: species entered as fixed when it should be a random factor, inflating degrees of freedom)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend mixed effects models when subjects/species/units are random samples from a population; specify random structure (e.g., treatment x species) and report rationale for model choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding causal overstatements
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the authors avoid claiming causality when data only support correlation? (Example: 'Last sentence ... suggests causality (“That is because…”) - but your data only support correlation')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors to temper causal language, rephrase to reflect correlational findings, and discuss alternative causal mechanisms or necessary experiments to establish causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation consistent with the strength of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the conclusions warranted by the data and analyses, and do authors avoid overreach? (Example: strong conclusions are not warranted due to fundamental concerns with design/analysis)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend scaling back conclusions if analyses are flawed, require additional analyses/experiments to support strong claims, and detail specific weaknesses that undermine conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures and captions clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Are figures and captions clear, complete, and statistically annotated? (Examples: missing stats for figures, unclear predictor choice in plots, suggestion to place linear equation in caption)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for inclusion of statistical tests and model summaries in captions, clarity on axes/units, and explanation for figure selections; request additional tables/figures if they would aid interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor versus major points separation and actionable suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the review separate major concerns (design/analysis) from minor revisions (text edits), and provide concrete, actionable suggestions? (Example structure: 'Minor points:' followed by specific fixes)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize feedback into major and minor points; for each major point, explain why it's important and suggest concrete remedies (reanalysis, additional controls, textual changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone, professionalism, and constructive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the review respectful, constructive, and professional while being candid? (Examples: 'I respect the authors’ patience and professionalism', balanced praise with critical analysis)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a collegial tone, acknowledge strengths before critiques, avoid ad hominem language, and offer to help clarify or collaborate where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of alternative explanations and suggested follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the review propose alternative interpretations and suggest follow-up experiments or analyses? (Examples: propose in vitro evolution experiments, suggest testing automated dispensing with Kir2.1 channels, propose randomization improvements)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer concrete experimental or analytical follow-ups that would address the reviewer's concerns or strengthen claims, and indicate which are essential versus optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical pedagogy and explanation when errors are technical
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the review explain technical/statistical errors and, where helpful, include exemplars or code to illustrate the point? (Example: reviewer included WinBUGS and MATLAB code to illustrate Bayesian and circular-analysis issues)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When technical issues are identified, provide clear explanation, references, and example code or pseudocode where feasible to aid authors' corrections. Encourage transparency in methods and reproducibility of analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation of data provenance and use of previously published data
rubrics_metrics.description: Are data sources and prior publications used for datasets clearly documented? (Example: indicate when some data come from previous studies and reference them appropriately)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask authors to specify which data were newly collected versus taken from prior work, provide references, and justify inclusion and comparability of compiled datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlighting strengths as well as weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the review clearly state the main strengths of the manuscript in addition to weaknesses? (Example language: 'The main strengths of this paper is that it addresses an interesting and timely question...')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance critique by enumerating novel contributions, robust parts of the work, and useful resources provided (e.g., data, adjustable figures), which helps authors and editors contextualize revisions.
